Warm-up + Sloth: Warm up progressively on easy climbing, then climb deliberately slowly. Pause in stable positions, place feet precisely, and avoid using momentum. The goal is movement control and body awareness, not fatigue.
Quiet Feet: Climb easy-to-moderate problems while making each foot placement nearly silent. Look at the foothold until the foot is placed, avoid scraping or readjusting, and prioritize precision over speed.
One Touch: Each hand or foot gets one deliberate placement on each hold. Once placed, do not shuffle or re-grip unless safety requires it. Preview the move before committing.
Flag Everything: On suitable moves, deliberately use a flag to counterbalance the body. Focus on where the free leg changes hip position, reach, and load on the hands.
Transfer: Apply the session's skill to normal climbing. Choose problems that let you use the skill without forcing it, and judge attempts by movement quality as well as completion.
Sloth: Climb substantially slower than normal. Maintain tension while moving between positions, pause when useful, and avoid jumping through weak positions.
One-leg climbing: Climb easy terrain while intentionally minimizing use of one leg, then switch sides. Use the drill to learn hip positioning, flagging, and how each leg contributes; keep difficulty low enough to stay controlled.
High-step/drop-knee transfer: Choose moves with a high foothold or useful drop-knee. Load the high foot, bring the hips toward it, rotate the hip/knee as the move requires, and stand through the leg rather than over-pulling with the arms.
Downclimb: Climb a problem or section up and then reverse the moves back down. Use deliberate foot placement and body positioning; choose terrain easy enough that the descent stays controlled.
Hover Hand: Before taking the next handhold, hover the reaching hand just off the hold for a brief moment. Maintain the position with the supporting arm, feet, and trunk, then complete the move without sagging.
Lock-off problem: Choose moves requiring a controlled bent-arm position. Establish the lock-off, keep the shoulder active and body positioned through the feet, then move the free hand without collapsing.
Limit bouldering: Work moves or short problems near your current maximum. Take few high-quality attempts with long rest, refine beta between attempts, and stop when power or movement quality clearly deteriorates.
Easy reset: Finish with a few easy, relaxed problems to restore smooth movement and reduce residual tension. Do not turn these into additional hard volume.
Wide reach stabilization: Choose a move that places the hands wider than usual. Reach into the wide position and stabilize the shoulders and trunk before continuing. Use challenging but controlled positions, never painful or unstable ones.
High-step/drop-knee: Practice a high-foot or drop-knee move deliberately. Set the foot first, organize the hips, then generate movement from the leg and hip rotation while keeping the upper body efficient.
Offset lock-off sequences: Use a short sequence where one arm carries more load than the other. Establish each offset lock-off under control, keep the shoulder active, then move through the sequence without rushing.
Deadpoint targets: Choose a target hold that requires a controlled dynamic reach. Generate force from legs and hips, release only as much tension as needed, and arrive with the hand as the body reaches its high point.
Dyno/coordination: Practice dynamic moves where both timing and body position matter. Use full rest, focus on takeoff direction and target contact, and stop before repeated attempts become slow or sloppy.
Limit power: Use very hard, low-repetition moves that require maximal speed or force. Rest fully between attempts and end the exercise when contact speed or explosiveness drops.
Easy finish: Do a small amount of easy climbing with relaxed movement after power work. It is a cooldown, not extra training volume.
Dynamic high-step/deadpoint: Set a high foot, load it quickly but accurately, and drive through the leg into a deadpoint. Coordinate hip extension with the reaching hand rather than pulling first with the arms.
Fast wide/offset lock-off acquisition: Move dynamically into a wide or offset hand position and stabilize it immediately. The goal is a fast catch followed by shoulder and trunk control, not hanging passively at end range.
Campus lunges OR bumps: On an appropriate campus board, use powerful controlled hand movements with adequate rest. Lunges move dynamically to a farther rung; bumps move a hand through successive rungs. Stop with any finger/shoulder pain or clear power loss.
Power primer: Use a very small number of hard, explosive boulders to recruit high force before endurance work. Rest enough that each attempt remains fast; do not accumulate fatigue here.
8–12 moderate moves → 2–4 hard moves: Climb a moderate sequence long enough to create some fatigue, then immediately enter a short hard crux. The purpose is producing difficult movement after accumulating pump.
Linked bouldering ~15–20 moves: Link problems or traverse sections to create a continuous 15–20-move effort. Choose difficulty that allows hard but repeatable rounds rather than immediate failure.
4×4 OR route intervals: For 4×4s, choose four manageable boulders and climb them in sequence with minimal rest, then recover between rounds. For route intervals, repeat sustained route/circuit efforts with planned rest. Use one protocol per session.
Crux-after-pump: Create moderate climbing first, then attempt a defined crux while fatigued. Keep the crux consistent enough to compare execution across rounds.
Technical transfer: After endurance work, climb a few easier problems while deliberately preserving foot precision and body position despite fatigue.
Warm-up + 1 limiter drill: Warm up progressively, then select one short drill addressing the day's most relevant limiter before project attempts. Keep the drill low-volume so it prepares rather than fatigues you.
Crux sections: Isolate the hardest section of a project. Rehearse individual moves and short links, refine beta, then gradually connect more of the section.
Serious project burns: Make full-intent attempts on the project with enough rest to preserve decision-making and power. Record beta, high point, failure reason, and useful changes after each burn.
Optional limiter drill: If quality remains high, finish with a small dose of a drill targeting the specific limiter exposed by the project. Skip it if fatigue would make the work low quality.
Pause & Plan: On moderate climbing, pause at selected stances before moving. Identify the next hand, foot, body position, and intended sequence, then execute the plan and compare it with what actually happened.
Project burns: Make high-quality attempts on the selected project with meaningful rest. Treat each burn as information: note beta, pacing, failure point, and whether the next attempt needs a technical or physical change.
Late-crux rehearsal: Use a longer sequence that places the target crux near the end. Practice arriving at the crux fatigued while preserving pacing, breathing, and the exact beta you intend to use.
Choose one emphasis for 2–3 weeks: Techn: Pick the weakness that outdoor climbing is currently undertraining and keep that emphasis for 2–3 weeks so it receives enough repeated exposure to adapt.
Technique: 4–6 moderate problems with Qu: Use moderate problems and combine precise feet, deliberate first placements, and a chosen body-position constraint. Difficulty should leave enough capacity to focus on execution.
Limit: 2–3 hard problems × 3–5 serious a: Choose 2–3 problems near your limit. Take 3–5 high-quality attempts on each with long rests and stop when attempts become meaningfully weaker.
Power: 2–3 dynamic problems × 3–4 + 2–3: Use a few dynamic problems plus targeted deadpoints. Rest fully, prioritize speed and contact quality, and stop before power declines.
Choose a complementary emphasis: Select a Wednesday focus that complements Monday and what outdoor climbing is providing, rather than duplicating the same stress.
Technique: 2–3 routes or 4–6 problems RP: Climb submaximally and use the session to reinforce efficient movement. Keep intensity moderate enough that technique remains the main constraint.
PE: 2–3 short 4×4/route-interval rounds: Use a small dose of power-endurance intervals. Finish each round significantly pumped but with enough quality to repeat the intended movement.
Project rehearsal: 2–4 burns or 2–3 long: Rehearse project-specific sequences with full-intent burns or longer links. Prioritize usable beta and repeatability rather than accumulating attempts.
Recovery skill: 30–45 min easy movement: Climb easy terrain continuously or in relaxed bouts. Focus on fluid movement, breathing, and technique; keep intensity low enough that you finish fresher rather than depleted.
Stop after 2 consecutive attempts with c: This is a stop rule, not an extra drill. End the power work once two attempts in a row show obvious loss of speed, coordination, or contact quality.
